The ACE Research Integrity Violations (ACE-RIV)

The ACE Research Integrity Violations is a classification system used to identify and categorize errors and integrity issues. It organizes existing standards from groups like Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), Council of Science Editors (CSE), International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), and The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA) into four main sections: Authorship and Publication, Statistical and Data Integrity, Publication Process Manipulation, and Ethical Oversight.

Each identified violation within the report will described clearly with evidence. For instance, if a statistical inconsistency is found, the report will detail the exact table or figure where the impossible data exists and explain why it is invalid. To provide a comprehensive overview, each report will open with an Executive Summary. This summary will feature a reference table that lists all violations in the report. Concluding the summary will be a clear, actionable recommendation, advising on the appropriate next steps, such as requesting raw data, issuing a retraction, or requesting a correction.

The list of violations are subject to change.

Section 1: Authorship and Publication

ACE 1.1: Guest, Honorary, or Gift Authorship

  • Standard: Authorship must be restricted to those who have made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research, avoiding inclusion based solely on a tenuous affiliation or an expectation that it will improve the chances of publication.
  • Source: Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Section 2.2.2; Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) Core Practice 2: Authorship and Contributorship.

ACE 1.2: Ghost Authorship

  • Standard: All individuals who actively participate in the research, data analysis, or manuscript drafting must be disclosed in the author byline or acknowledgments, preventing the undisclosed involvement of industry employees, medical writers, or marketing staff.
  • Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.2.2; COPE Core Practice 2: Authorship and Contributorship.

ACE 1.3: Authorship for Sale and Paper Mill Activity

  • Standard: The buying or selling of authorship positions on a scientific manuscript is explicitly prohibited. The use of commercial paper mills that organize on-demand writing of fraudulent academic manuscripts and offer co-authorship for sale represents a severe breach of research integrity.
  • Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.2.2; Researcher Connect; COPE & STM Paper Mills Report.

ACE 1.4: Plagiarism

  • Standard: The inclusion of other people’s work or ideas without providing proper credit to the original source.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines.

Section 2: Statistical and Data Integrity

ACE 2.1: Anomalies and Extreme Values

  • Standard: The reporting of data, statistics, or results that display extreme or unrealistic values, highly improbable distributions, or terminal digit frequencies that are inconsistent with random processes. Such anomalies suggest deviations from expected observations.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); Brookes (2024) Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons.

ACE 2.2: Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets

  • Standard: The presence of irreconcilable mathematical discrepancies within the reported data or summary statistics. This includes the reporting of statistical combinations (e.g., means, standard deviations, and sample sizes) that are mathematically impossible to derive from any empirical dataset, or outcomes that are fundamentally incompatible with the stated methodology.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); CSE White Paper, Section 3.4.1; Brookes (2024) Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons.

ACE 2.3: Selective Reporting, Suppressed Data, and Omitted Methodology

  • Standard: The selective publication of research outcomes, characterized by the unjustifiable omission or suppression of data, negative results, or conflicting findings that are relevant to the study’s conclusions. In the context of clinical research, this includes, but is not limited to, the failure to report all primary and secondary outcomes as they were originally prospectively registered in a clinical trial registry. Additionally this integrity standard includes the withholding of methodological details, experimental procedures, or analytical procedures necessary for the independent verification and reproducibility of the results.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work; Singapore Statement on Research Integrity.

ACE 2.4: Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting

  • Standard: The inaccurate calculation, transcription, or reporting of quantitative data and statistical results. This encompasses observable calculation errors, discrepancies between presented raw data and derived summary statistics, and the misuse of statistical methods to inappropriately suggest or alter statistical significance.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); Brookes (Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons); Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).

Section 3: Publication Process Manipulation

ACE 3.1: Duplicate Publication and Salami Slicing

  • Standard: Authors must avoid duplicate publication by not reproducing verbatim content from their own previously published work. Additionally, chopping up research results into multiple smaller papers with the specific aim of artificially increasing publication counts (“salami publications”) is an unacceptable practice.
  • Source: Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Section 2.2.6; The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); ICMJE Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals, Section III.D.2; COPE Core Practice 7: Intellectual Property.

ACE 3.2: Citation Manipulation

  • Standard: Any systematic practice that inappropriately pressures authors to cite material with the primary goal of boosting citation rates.
  • Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.1.5; The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines

ACE 3.3: Peer Review Subversion

  • Standard: The manipulation of the peer review process, such as participating in groups of reviewers and authors colluding to review each other’s publications, undermines the quality control of research. The exchange of payment for the allowance of fake reviewer reports is a known predatory practice.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines; Patterns of Paper Mill Papers and Retraction Challenges (Peer Review Congress); COPE Core Practice 9: Peer Review Processes

Section 4: Ethical Oversight and Transparency

ACE 4.1: Failure to Disclose Conflicts of Interest (COI)

  • Standard: Researchers should clearly disclose any financial and other conflicts of interest that could compromise the trustworthiness of their work in research proposals, publications, and public communications.
  • Source: Singapore Statement on Research Integrity, Principle 9; Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Sections 2.1.3 & 2.1.4; COPE Core Practice 4: Conflicts of Interest / Competing Interests; ICMJE Recommendations and Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest; Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).

ACE 4.2: Evasion of Ethical Oversight

  • Standard: Researchers must handle research participants and subjects with respect and care, and strictly in accordance with legal provisions and ethical principles.
  • Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA), Section 2.4; Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Sections 2.2.6 & 3.1.1; COPE Core Practice 6: Ethical Oversight; Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).
